The parables serve to unveil the mysteries of the kingdom of God while hiding these truths from hardened hearts, inviting deeper reflection on our disposition to receive the word of God.
35.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of spiritual searching and humility in our quest for truth. Jesus' parables encourage us to meditate on the teachings of the Bible and seek to understand the depths of divine wisdom. As believers, we are called to open our hearts and receive these revelations, in order to live fully according to the principles of the kingdom of God.

mots.sens: This term refers to a comparison or metaphor, often used by Jesus to teach deep spiritual truths through simple stories. The root of the word evokes the idea of placing side by side, thus allowing for understanding through analogy. In the context of Matthew 13, the parable is a means for Jesus to reveal hidden truths about the kingdom of heaven while preserving a certain obscurity for those who are not receptive.

This word means 'house' and refers to a place of residence, but in a broader sense, it can symbolize the community or body of believers. In the context of this passage, the house represents a space of revelation and teaching, where the disciples can draw closer to Jesus to understand the mysteries of the kingdom. This underscores the importance of communion and intimacy in the pursuit of spiritual truth.

This term means 'disciples' and refers to those who follow a master to learn from him. The disciples of Jesus are called to a relationship of learning and transformation, seeking to understand and live according to his teachings. In this verse, their request for explanation shows their desire to deepen their faith and understanding of spiritual truths.

36.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, at a time when Jesus preached in a Jewish context, with strong messianic expectations and an agricultural society. The parables were an effective means of communicating spiritual truths to an audience that understood the realities of daily life.
36.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus teaches through several parables about the kingdom of heaven. After sharing the parable of the weeds, he withdraws with his disciples to explain the hidden meaning of his teachings, emphasizing the importance of spiritual understanding.
36.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued teaching through stories and parables. This allowed for the transmission of moral and spiritual lessons in an accessible manner, while engaging the audience to reflect deeply on the implications of these narratives.
36.interpretation: The disciples' request for an explanation of the parable of the weeds reveals their desire to deepen their understanding of the truths of the kingdom. It also illustrates that spiritual revelation requires active seeking and a willingness to learn. Jesus uses this opportunity to teach about the coexistence of good and evil in the world until the end of time.
36.commentaire: This passage encourages us to seek a deeper understanding of Jesus' teachings. Like the disciples, we are called to approach him with an open heart, eager to learn and grow in our faith. It also reminds us that, even in a world where evil seems to prosper, God has a plan and a promise of justice at the end of time.

mots.sens: This term refers to 'seed' in both a literal and figurative sense. In the agricultural context, it refers to the seed that, when sown, produces a harvest. Spiritually, it evokes the word of God which, when received in the heart, brings forth eternal life. Thus, the good seed represents the teaching and work of Christ in the lives of believers.

This expression, translated as 'Son of Man', is a messianic reference that emphasizes the humanity of Jesus while affirming his divine authority. It also evokes Christ's mission on earth, embodying both suffering and glory. In this verse, it highlights that it is through him that truth and life are sown into the world.

37.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman occupation, and the Jewish people were awaiting a Messiah who would liberate Israel. Jesus, as the Son of Man, presents himself as the one who brings a new understanding of the kingdom of God.
37.passage: This verse is part of a series of parables that Jesus uses to teach about the kingdom of heaven. Chapter 13 of Matthew is centered on the revelation of the mysteries of the kingdom through simple yet profound stories.
37.culture: In Jewish culture, agriculture was a common metaphor for illustrating spiritual truths. Farmers understood well the importance of seed and soil, making Jesus' teachings accessible and relevant to his audience.
37.interpretation: Jesus, as the Son of Man, is the one who sows the good seed, that is, the word of God. This underscores the importance of receiving and cultivating this seed in our hearts to produce spiritual fruit.
37.commentaire: This verse reminds us that the word of God, sown in our lives, has the power to transform and give life. As disciples, we are called to receive this seed and share it with others, thereby contributing to the expansion of the kingdom of God on earth.

mots.sens: The term 'kosmos' refers to the entirety of creation, the world in its entirety. It evokes not only the physical earth but also the order and structure of human life. In the context of this verse, it symbolizes the realm in which believers and non-believers coexist, highlighting the reality of the spiritual struggle between good and evil in the world.

The word 'sporos' means seed and refers to the idea of potential and growth. In the agricultural culture of the time, seed was essential for producing fruit. Spiritually, this refers to the sons of the kingdom who, as seed, carry within them the potential for eternal life and transformation, called to grow in faith.

The term 'zizanion' refers to tares, a harmful plant that resembles wheat in its youth. This word emphasizes the deception and coexistence of evil with good. Theologically, it reminds us that in the world, evil may appear similar to good, but it is destined to be separated and judged at the end of time.

The word 'huioi' means sons and refers to a relationship of belonging and identity. In this verse, it designates those who are born of God and who live according to His principles. This underscores the idea that the sons of the kingdom are called to represent the character of God in the world, in contrast to the sons of the evil one.

38.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the first century, where Jesus taught in a Jewish environment under Roman occupation, a time of great messianic expectation and religious tensions.
38.passage: Matthew 13 is part of Jesus' parables, where he uses agricultural images to teach deep spiritual truths about the kingdom of God. This verse is part of the parable of the tares, illustrating the reality of the coexistence of good and evil in the world.
38.culture: In Jewish culture, agriculture was central to daily life, and agricultural metaphors were commonly used to teach spiritual truths. Seed and harvest symbolize God's promise and the coming judgment.
38.interpretation: This verse reveals the dual nature of the world, where the sons of the kingdom and the sons of the evil one coexist. It emphasizes the importance of discerning between the true and the false, while reminding us that final judgment will come to separate the good grain from the tares.
38.commentaire: As believers, we are called to be sons of the kingdom, carrying the good seed in a world filled with tares. This reminds us of our responsibility to live according to the values of the kingdom of God, while having the wisdom to discern the malignant influences around us. By cultivating our faith and witnessing the love of Christ, we contribute to the growth of the kingdom of God in this world.

mots.sens: This term means 'accuser' or 'slanderer.' It is derived from the verb 'diaballo,' which means 'to divide' or 'to separate.' In the context of this verse, the devil is presented as the enemy who sows discord and evil in the world. Theologically, this underscores the reality of evil and the spiritual opposition to God's work in the lives of believers.

This word refers to 'harvest,' a term that evokes the gathering of the fruits of labor. It is often used in Scripture to symbolize the final judgment and the separation between good and evil. In this verse, it emphasizes the importance of the end times, where every action will be judged and the righteous will be distinguished from the unrighteous.

Meaning 'messenger,' this term is used to refer to angels, spiritual beings sent by God to accomplish His will. In the context of this verse, the angels are the agents of the harvest, symbolizing divine justice that is executed at the end of times. This reminds believers that God uses spiritual means to fulfill His plan of redemption and judgment.

39.epoque: This passage was written in a first-century Jewish context, where believers were awaiting the coming of the Messiah and the fulfillment of God's promises. Jesus' teachings were often in opposition to the established religious traditions of the time.
39.passage: In this chapter, Jesus teaches through parables, revealing deep truths about the kingdom of heaven. This verse is part of the explanation of the parable of the weeds, where He clarifies the reality of evil in the world and God's role in the final judgment.
39.culture: The Jewish culture of the time was heavily influenced by eschatological expectations, with a strong belief in a final judgment and the separation of the righteous and the unrighteous. Farmers were well acquainted with the process of sowing and harvesting, making the parable particularly relevant.
39.interpretation: This verse highlights the spiritual struggle between good and evil, emphasizing that the devil is the source of corruption in the world. The harvest represents the moment when God will intervene to establish His kingdom, and the angels will play a crucial role in this final separation.
39.commentaire: This passage reminds us that, although evil may seem to prosper, God has a plan for redemption and judgment. As believers, we are called to remain vigilant and discern the influences of evil in our lives. This encourages us to live in accordance with the truth of the Gospel, knowing that our faithfulness will be rewarded at the final harvest.

mots.sens: This term refers to a harmful plant, often interpreted as tares, which resembles wheat in its youth. In the biblical context, tares symbolize evil and false believers who coexist with true disciples of Christ. The root of this word evokes the idea of confusion and deception, highlighting the need for spiritual discernment at the end of times.

This verb means 'to burn completely' and is used to describe the action of destroying by fire. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the ultimate judgment awaiting those considered as tares, symbolizing the definitive separation between good and evil. Theologically, this recalls God's justice that purifies and eliminates sin.

This word means 'end' or 'goal,' and in this context, it refers to the conclusion of human history and the fulfillment of the divine plan. It indicates that the world as we know it will come to a conclusion, where judgment will be rendered. This underscores the importance of living in accordance with God's will in view of this end.

40.epoque: The historical context of this passage is situated in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Palestine, where He teaches a people confronted with messianic expectations and spiritual struggles.
40.passage: This verse is part of a parable about the good grain and the tares, where Jesus explains the coexistence of the righteous and the wicked until the end of times. It emphasizes the importance of discernment and divine judgment at the end of the world.
40.culture: In the agricultural culture of the time, the separation of wheat and tares was a daily reality, making the parable particularly relevant for Jesus' listeners, allowing them to understand deep spiritual truths through familiar images.
40.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse reminds us that God's judgment is inevitable and that, although evil may temporarily prosper, it will ultimately be destroyed. This calls us to remain vigilant and identify ourselves as the good grain, living according to Christ's teachings.
40.commentaire: This passage urges us to reflect on our own lives and faith. Are we authentic witnesses of Christ, or does our life allow room for tares? While awaiting the end of times, we are called to live in the light, to purify ourselves, and to bear fruit, knowing that God is just and will separate the good from the bad.

mots.sens: This term refers to that which causes a fall or an obstacle, often used to describe behaviors or teachings that lead others into sin. In the biblical context, scandals are elements that disrupt the harmony of the kingdom of God. Spiritually, this underscores the responsibility of believers to live in a way that is not a stumbling block for others.

This word literally means 'without law' and refers to iniquity or the absence of respect for divine laws. It evokes a rebellion against the moral order established by God. In this verse, it highlights the seriousness of actions that oppose divine will and their consequences in the final judgment.

This term means 'kingdom' and refers to God's reign on earth and in the hearts of believers. It implies divine authority and a spiritual order. The notion of kingdom in this verse reminds us that God has a plan to establish justice and eliminate evil, which is central to Jesus' teaching.

41.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman rule, and the Jews were awaiting a Messiah who would establish an earthly kingdom. Jesus' teachings, centered on the kingdom of God, challenged the traditional Jewish expectations regarding justice and judgment.
41.passage: This verse is situated in the chapter where Jesus teaches through parables about the kingdom of heaven. He describes the final judgment and the separation between the righteous and the wicked, emphasizing the necessity of a life in accordance with God's will.
41.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of judgment and purification was very present. Believers were called to prepare for the day of the Lord, a concept that involved both hope and fear, depending on their faithfulness to divine law.
41.interpretation: This passage emphasizes that the Son of Man, Jesus, has the authority to judge and purify His kingdom. The angels, as messengers of God, will play an active role in this separation, indicating that judgment is inevitable and that divine justice will be established.
41.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of our conduct as members of the kingdom of God. We must be vigilant not to become stumbling blocks for others. By living according to the principles of God's word, we contribute to the building of His kingdom and the honor of His name.

mots.sens: This term literally means 'bosom' or 'hollow', but in a spiritual context, it evokes the idea of a place of refuge or protection. In the context of this verse, it can symbolize the place where the righteous are gathered, in contrast to the fiery furnace. The theological significance here emphasizes the separation between salvation and perdition, highlighting the necessity of an authentic relationship with God.

This word means 'fire' and is often used in Scripture to symbolize divine judgment. The fire here is not only a physical punishment but also a spiritual purification, representing God's anger against sin. The spiritual significance of this term reminds believers of the seriousness of judgment and the importance of living according to divine precepts.

This word translates to 'weeping' and evokes deep sadness or intense grief. In this verse, it describes the suffering of the lost, underscoring the reality of despair that accompanies the rejection of God. Spiritually, this reminds us of the importance of repentance and seeking divine grace to avoid such a fate.

This term means 'grinding' and is often associated with the idea of pain and torment. In the context of this verse, it represents the anguish and regret of lost souls. This underscores the tragic consequence of choosing to live outside of God's will, calling us to a life of vigilance and faithfulness.

42.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, at a time when Jesus was teaching in a Jewish context, confronted with messianic expectations and profound spiritual realities.
42.passage: This verse is part of a series of parables that Jesus uses to explain the kingdom of heaven. It illustrates the final separation between the righteous and the wicked, highlighting the reality of the coming judgment.
42.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the idea of the fiery furnace was well understood as a symbol of divine judgment, reinforcing the necessity of a life in accordance with God's laws.
42.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God's judgment is inevitable and that the separation between good and evil is real. It calls us to reflect on our own spiritual state and our relationship with Christ.
42.commentaire: This passage urges us to take seriously the consequences of our spiritual choices. As believers, we are called to live in the light and to share the Gospel, so that others may avoid the fiery furnace. The promise of eternal life in Christ encourages us to remain faithful and to seek to glorify God in all our actions.

mots.sens: This term means 'righteous' or 'just'. It designates those who are in accordance with God's will, having been declared righteous by faith in Christ. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the divine reward reserved for those who live according to the principles of the kingdom of God, highlighting their spiritual transformation and eternal inheritance.

This word means 'ray' or 'light'. It evokes the idea of brilliance and splendor, symbolizing divine glory. In this verse, it is used to describe how the righteous will shine, underscoring their participation in God's glory and their reflection of divine light in the heavenly kingdom.

This term means 'kingdom' and refers to the sovereignty and kingship of God. It represents God's reign over the hearts of believers and the future establishment of His kingdom. In this passage, it emphasizes the eschatological hope of believers, who will live in the fullness of this eternal kingship.

This word means 'father' and expresses an intimate and personal relationship. In the Christian context, it refers to God as the heavenly Father, implying love, protection, and guidance. This underscores the identity of believers as children of God, called to live in communion with Him in His kingdom.

43.epoque: This passage was written in a 1st century Jewish context, where Jesus' teachings clashed with established religious traditions and the messianic expectations of the people of Israel.
43.passage: Matthew 13 is part of the parables of Jesus, where He teaches about the kingdom of heaven. Verse 43 concludes a series of parables about judgment and the separation between the righteous and the unrighteous.
43.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of resurrection and eschatological reward was central. The righteous were expected to receive a reward in the world to come, which resonates deeply in Jesus' teaching.
43.interpretation: This verse promises that the righteous, those who have followed Christ, will shine with the glory of God in His kingdom. This emphasizes not only their salvation but also their transformation and glorification as children of God.
43.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our faith in Christ assures us a place in the kingdom of God, where we will share in His glory. It encourages us to live according to the principles of justice and truth, knowing that our destiny is to shine like stars in eternity. Let us be witnesses of this light in our daily lives, reflecting the love and justice of our heavenly Father.

mots.sens: This word means 'treasure' and evokes precious wealth, often hidden or protected. In the context of this verse, it symbolizes the kingdom of heaven, which is of inestimable value. The discovery of a hidden treasure implies a divine revelation, highlighting the importance of seeking and finding what is spiritually precious.

This term means 'joy' and expresses a state of deep and lasting happiness. In this passage, the joy of the man who finds the treasure underscores the great value of the kingdom of heaven. This joy is a spiritual response to the discovery of divine truth and eternal life.

This verb means 'to buy' and implies an exchange of value. In the context of this verse, it represents the sacrifice one is willing to make to acquire the kingdom of heaven. This underscores the idea that entering the kingdom requires a conscious decision and total commitment.

44.epoque: This passage was written in a 1st century Jewish context, where Jesus' teachings resonated with the messianic expectations and religious traditions of the time.
44.passage: Matthew 13 is part of a series of parables that Jesus uses to teach about the kingdom of heaven. This verse illustrates the supreme value of the kingdom and the appropriate response to this discovery.
44.culture: In Jewish culture, the possession of land and treasures was highly valued, and the discovery of a hidden treasure would have been considered a divine blessing. This reinforces the idea that the kingdom of heaven is an invaluable spiritual wealth.
44.interpretation: The parable teaches that the kingdom of heaven is of such great value that it deserves all sacrifices. The joy of the discoverer shows that the Christian life is a source of happiness and fulfillment when one chooses to follow Christ.
44.commentaire: This verse calls us to evaluate our priorities and recognize the value of the kingdom of God in our lives. Like this man, we must be willing to forsake our earthly possessions to acquire what is eternal. The joy that accompanies this discovery reminds us that the path of faith is a source of true happiness.

mots.sens: This word refers to a pearl, often considered precious and rare. In the biblical context, pearls symbolize beauty, value, and wisdom. Spiritually, they can represent the truth and knowledge of the kingdom of God, which are both precious and to be sought diligently.

This term means merchant or trader, designating a person engaged in commerce. The merchant in this parable represents someone with a purpose, actively seeking something valuable. This emphasizes the idea that the kingdom of heaven requires active searching and a fervent desire to discover spiritual riches.

45.epoque: In the first century, Jewish society was marked by messianic expectations and a strong commercial tradition, with exchanges of precious goods like pearls.
45.passage: This verse is found in the chapter of parables in Matthew, where Jesus teaches about the nature of the kingdom of heaven through images accessible to His audience, highlighting the priceless value of this kingdom.
45.culture: In Jewish culture, pearls were considered treasures and symbolized wisdom and beauty. The search for pearls evokes the idea of quest and value, concepts deeply rooted in Jewish spirituality.
45.interpretation: This parable illustrates the search for the kingdom of heaven, which is of supreme value. Like the merchant seeking pearls, believers are called to actively seek the truth and relationship with God, recognizing the spiritual wealth it brings.
45.commentaire: This verse reminds us that the kingdom of heaven is not simply a gift offered, but a treasure to be sought with passion. As Christians, we must be like this merchant, determined to discover and seize the divine truths that transform our lives. This prompts us to evaluate our priorities and invest our time and efforts in what has eternal value.

mots.sens: This word means 'pearl' and evokes an invaluable worth and rare beauty. In the biblical context, it often symbolizes divine wisdom and knowledge. The pearl is also a symbol of purity and perfection, representing the kingdom of heaven, which the believer must seek diligently.

This term means 'to buy' and implies an act of deliberate choice and sacrifice. It evokes the idea of redeeming something precious, often at a high cost. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of making choices that reflect our eternal priorities, setting aside earthly things to acquire what is truly valuable.

This word means 'all' and emphasizes the idea of totality and complete commitment. In this context, it indicates that the individual is willing to give up everything they possess to obtain the pearl of great price. This challenges us regarding our own commitment to the kingdom of God, calling us to a wholehearted devotion.

46.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context where Judaism and the early Christian communities sought to understand and live out faith in Jesus Christ in the face of cultural and religious challenges.
46.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus teaches through parables, revealing profound truths about the kingdom of heaven. The parable of the pearl of great price highlights the priceless value of the kingdom and the commitment required to enter it.
46.culture: In the Jewish and Mediterranean culture of the time, pearls were considered rare and precious treasures, often associated with wealth and beauty. This accentuates the importance of the merchant's decision in the parable.
46.interpretation: This parable illustrates the nature of the kingdom of heaven, which is of supreme value, surpassing all that one can possess. It calls us to evaluate our priorities and be ready to make sacrifices to enter this divine reality.
46.commentaire: The verse reminds us that the kingdom of God requires total commitment and an evaluation of our values. Just as the merchant sold all he had to acquire the pearl, we are called to renounce our earthly attachments to embrace eternal life in Christ. This pushes us to reflect on what we consider precious in our lives and to ardently seek what is truly important.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to throw around' or 'to cast into'. In the context of this verse, it evokes the action of casting a net into the sea, symbolizing evangelism and the gathering of souls. The theological significance lies in the idea that God, through His Church, actively engages in gathering the lost, without distinction, to bring them into His kingdom.

This term means 'fish'. In Christian culture, the fish is a symbol of Christ and believers, representing the community of the faithful. The diversity of fish caught in the net symbolizes the variety of people that God calls to Himself, illustrating the inclusive nature of the kingdom of heaven.

This word means 'kingdom'. It denotes the sovereignty of God and the spiritual authority that governs the hearts of believers. In this verse, it emphasizes that the kingdom of heaven is a dynamic reality, where individuals from all backgrounds are invited to enter into relationship with God, reinforcing the idea that the kingdom is accessible to all.

47.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in a context where Jesus teaches Jews and Gentiles about the nature of the kingdom of God, using metaphors understandable to His audience.
47.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus uses parables to reveal profound truths about the kingdom of heaven. This verse is part of a series of comparisons that illustrate the diversity and breadth of the divine call.
47.culture: In Jesus' time, fishing was a common and essential activity for sustenance, and the net was a symbolic tool of gathering. The listeners easily understood the image of the net to illustrate God's work in the world.
47.interpretation: This verse reminds us that the kingdom of heaven is open to all, without distinction. The net represents evangelism, where each soul is precious and invited to enter the community of believers, highlighting God's inclusive love.
47.commentaire: The verse calls us to be fishers of men, to share the Gospel with all those around us. As members of the Church, we must commit to gathering the lost, remembering that each person has immeasurable value in God's eyes. Let us be attentive to opportunities to witness our faith and invite others to discover the kingdom of heaven.

mots.sens: This word means 'fish' and is used in the context of fishing. In Jewish culture, fish often symbolize life and prosperity, but here it also represents God's judgment on humanity. The act of sorting the fish evokes the separation between the righteous and the unrighteous, a central theme in Jesus' teachings.

This term means 'good' or 'virtuous'. In the context of this verse, it refers to the fish that are deemed worthy to be kept. This raises questions about the nature of goodness and divine justice, highlighting the idea that God values what is good and useful for His kingdom.

This word means 'bad' or 'evil'. In this passage, it refers to the fish that are rejected. This underscores the principle of divine judgment, where what is evil is cast aside, reminding us of the importance of living according to God's standards to avoid being rejected.

48.epoque: This passage was written in the context of the 1st century, during a time when the Jewish people were under Roman rule and seeking spiritual and messianic answers. Jesus' teachings were directed at an audience well-versed in Jewish traditions and messianic expectations.
48.passage: This verse is part of the parable of the net, where Jesus teaches about the kingdom of heaven. Matthew chapter 13 contains several parables that illustrate the nature of God's kingdom, its growth, and its final judgment.
48.culture: In Jewish culture, fishing was a common and symbolic activity. Fishermen were often seen as figures of the community, and the sorting of fish evokes themes of purity and separation, which were important in Mosaic law.
48.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse illustrates God's final judgment, where the righteous will be separated from the unrighteous. It reminds us that our actions and faith determine our place in God's kingdom, and that we must live in accordance with His precepts.
48.commentaire: This passage calls us to reflect on our own lives and our relationship with God. It reminds us that, just as fishermen sort the fish, God will judge our actions and our hearts. Therefore, let us be vigilant and seek to be 'fish' that please God, living according to His word and doing good around us.

mots.sens: The term 'ἄγγελοι' refers to messengers, often in reference to God's angels. Their role is to serve and execute divine will, which includes the separation of the righteous and the wicked at the end of time. In the eschatological context, this word emphasizes God's authority and power to judge, as well as the importance of divine justice.

The word 'δικαῖοι' means 'righteous' and refers to those who are in accordance with God's will. This implies not only a moral position but also a right relationship with God, acquired through faith in Christ. In this verse, it underscores the promise of redemption and reward for those who live according to divine principles.

The term 'πονηροί' translates to 'wicked' and designates those who act against God's will. This word implies a perverse nature and opposition to divine justice. In the context of this verse, it highlights the inevitable judgment awaiting those who choose to live in sin and rebellion.

49.epoque: The historical context of this passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by Roman occupation and religious tensions among various Jewish sects.
49.passage: This verse is part of a series of parables that Jesus uses to teach about the kingdom of heaven. In this chapter, He speaks about the realities of final judgment and the separation between the righteous and the wicked, thus illustrating the nature of God's kingdom.
49.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of judgment and separation at the end of times was deeply rooted, with expectations regarding the coming of a Messiah who would establish justice. Angels were often perceived as God's agents in executing His judgment.
49.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the certainty of a final judgment where the righteous will be separated from the wicked, a spiritual reality that reminds us of the importance of living according to God's principles. It highlights God's sovereignty in judgment and the ultimate retribution for human actions.
49.commentaire: Matthew 13:49 reminds us that life on earth is temporary and that our choices have eternal consequences. As believers, we are called to live in accordance with God's will, knowing that we will be held accountable for our actions. This passage encourages us to pray for the wicked and to share the Gospel, so that they too may know God's grace and justice.

mots.sens: This term designates a place of eternal punishment, often associated with the punishment of the wicked. Etymologically, it comes from the Valley of Hinnom, a place where sacrifices were offered to idols and where fires burned continuously. In the biblical context, it symbolizes eternal separation from God, representing the ultimate consequence of rejecting His grace.

This word means 'weeping' or 'lamentation', and it evokes deep sadness and intense grief. It is often used in Scripture to describe the suffering of lost souls. In this verse, it underscores the pain and despair that accompany final judgment, reminding believers of the seriousness of spiritual choices.

This term translates to 'gnashing of teeth', symbolizing anger, frustration, and despair. It is associated with an intense reaction of suffering in the face of loss and regret. In the context of this verse, it illustrates the tragic reality of souls who realize the gravity of their separation from God.

50.epoque: This passage was written in the 1st century, in a context where Jesus' teachings often confronted traditional Jewish beliefs and messianic expectations.
50.passage: Matthew 13 deals with the parables of the kingdom of heaven, where Jesus teaches about the nature of judgment and the separation between the righteous and the unrighteous at the end of times.
50.culture: In Jewish culture, the images of Gehenna and eternal punishment were well-known and served as a warning about the consequences of sin and rejection of God.
50.interpretation: This verse highlights the reality of final judgment, where the wicked will be separated from the righteous. The fiery furnace represents a powerful metaphor for eternal suffering, emphasizing the importance of living in accordance with Christ's teachings.
50.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the gravity of the spiritual choice each person must make. As believers, we are called to proclaim the Gospel and warn those who do not yet know Christ of the consequences of their rejection. It urges us to live a life of holiness and to testify to God's love, so that others may escape this tragic destiny.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to understand' or 'to have a clear knowledge.' It evokes an understanding that goes beyond mere recognition, involving a deep perception of spiritual truths. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the importance of fully grasping the teachings of Jesus, which has implications for faith and Christian life.

This word means 'all' or 'everything.' It indicates the universality and completeness of the teachings that Jesus shared. In this context, it emphasizes that the disciples not only understood isolated truths but the entirety of Jesus' message, which is crucial for their future mission.

51.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, in a context where Jesus was teaching in Galilee, a place of cultural and religious diversity, where messianic expectations were high.
51.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus uses parables to reveal deep truths about the kingdom of heaven. This verse concludes a series of teachings where the disciples are invited to understand the scope of these truths.
51.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued teaching and understanding of the Scriptures. The disciples, by responding affirmatively, show their commitment to Jesus' teaching, which was essential for their role in spreading the Gospel.
51.interpretation: Jesus' question highlights the importance of spiritual understanding. The disciples affirm that they have grasped the truths he taught, which prepares them to be effective witnesses. It also indicates that understanding Christ's teachings is an active and ongoing process.
51.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of seeking to understand Jesus' teachings in our daily lives. As modern disciples, we are called not only to hear but to fully grasp the truths of God's Word. This compels us to deepen our faith and share these teachings with others.

mots.sens: This term designates a scribe, a person educated in the Law and the Scriptures. Scribes were often teachers and interpreters of sacred texts, having a deep knowledge of Jewish traditions and writings. In this verse, the scribe is compared to a householder, emphasizing the importance of his ability to convey both old and new teachings, which is essential for understanding the kingdom of heaven.

This word means treasure or reserve, and it evokes the idea of accumulated wealth. In the biblical context, it can refer to wisdom, teachings, and spiritual truths that one can draw from. The scribe's treasure represents both ancient knowledge (the Scriptures) and new (the revelations of Christ), highlighting the importance of integrating these two dimensions into Christian life.

This word means new, but in a sense that implies a renewed quality or a newness of nature. It is often used in the New Testament to designate the realities of the kingdom of God that are revealed by Christ. In this verse, it emphasizes that the understanding of the kingdom of heaven is not merely a repetition of old truths, but a dynamic and living revelation that transforms the lives of believers.

This term means old or ancient, and it is often used to refer to things that have historical or traditional value. In the context of this verse, it refers to the established teachings and truths of the Old Testament. The combination of old and new things in the scribe's treasure shows that God's revelation is a continuum, linking the Old and New Testaments.

52.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by religious and political tensions, where the teachings of rabbis and scribes played a central role in the spiritual life of the Jews.
52.passage: In this chapter, Jesus teaches through parables, revealing deep truths about the kingdom of heaven. Verse 52 concludes these teachings by highlighting the crucial role of educated scribes in transmitting these truths.
52.culture: In Jesus' time, scribes were respected as religious authorities and teachers. Their role was to preserve and interpret the Scriptures, which conferred upon them great responsibility in the spiritual formation of the people.
52.interpretation: This verse highlights the importance of knowledge and teaching in Christian life. The educated scribe is one who knows how to draw from the riches of God's Word, both old and new, to nourish and build up the faith community.
52.commentaire: This passage reminds us that the Christian faith is rooted in ancient Scriptures while being enlivened by the revelations of Christ. As believers, we are called to be like educated scribes, seeking to understand and share the richness of divine truth, in order to build the kingdom of God in our lives and in our surroundings.

mots.sens: The term 'παραβολή' designates a comparison or metaphor, often used to teach deep spiritual truths. Its primary meaning involves the idea of juxtaposition, where a simple story illuminates a more complex reality. In the context of this verse, it underscores the importance of Jesus' teachings, which use accessible narratives to reveal divine truths. Theologically, this shows that God reveals Himself to us through understandable means.

This word means 'to release' or 'to depart,' and in this context, it indicates that Jesus has completed his teaching and is about to leave the place where he was. This evokes a notion of conclusion and transition, marking a moment where the listeners must reflect on the teachings received. Spiritually, this can symbolize that, after receiving the truth, it is time for each of us to put into practice what we have learned.

The verb 'ἔχω' means 'to have' or 'to possess,' and in this context, it can be interpreted as Jesus having 'completed' his parables. This emphasizes the fullness of his teaching, as if he had given all that was necessary to understand the kingdom of God. Theologically, this reminds us that Christ's word is complete and sufficient to guide our lives.

53.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, at a time when Jesus was teaching in Israel, confronted with established religious traditions and a people in search of truth.
53.passage: This verse concludes a series of parables that Jesus has shared to reveal the nature of the kingdom of heaven. It marks a turning point in his ministry, where he begins to withdraw from the crowds to focus on his disciples.
53.culture: In Jewish culture, parables were a common means of teaching, using images from everyday life to convey spiritual truths. This made the teachings accessible and memorable for the listeners.
53.interpretation: This verse underscores the importance of Jesus' teaching and the moment when he withdraws after sharing profound truths. It reminds us that each of Christ's teachings is an invitation to reflection and application in our daily lives.
53.commentaire: By concluding his parables, Jesus calls us to take his teachings seriously. We must not only listen but also act accordingly, integrating these truths into our lives. This moment of departure reminds us that divine wisdom is available to us, and it is up to us to seize it and put it into practice.

mots.sens: This term refers to wisdom, a deep and practical understanding of the realities of life. In the biblical context, wisdom is often associated with the fear of God and the ability to apply spiritual truths in daily life. Here, it emphasizes Jesus' authority as a teacher, capable of revealing divine truths that surpass human understanding.

This word means miracles or wonders, indicating extraordinary events that testify to divine power. In the New Testament, the miracles of Jesus serve not only to heal and deliver but also to confirm his messianic identity. They often provoke astonishment and questions about the source of this power, as here, where the listeners wonder about the source of Jesus' miracles.

This term refers to homeland or native land, highlighting the importance of cultural and familial roots. In the context of this verse, it underscores the fact that Jesus returned to his own environment, where expectations and prejudices can influence the reception of his message. It reminds us that even in our own settings, familiarity can sometimes breed contempt or disbelief.

54.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where the synagogue was a central place of teaching and gathering for the Jews.
54.passage: In this chapter, Jesus teaches through parables and begins to reveal the nature of his ministry. His return to his homeland highlights the contrast between the warm welcome he receives elsewhere and the skepticism of those who have known him since childhood.
54.culture: Jewish culture valued teaching in synagogues, and rabbis were respected for their wisdom. However, familiarity with Jesus as the son of the carpenter made it difficult for some to recognize his divine authority.
54.interpretation: This verse illustrates the tension between Jesus' divine wisdom and the disbelief of those who know him. It reminds us that faith does not solely depend on intellectual knowledge but on an open disposition to receive God's revelation, even from those we consider familiar.
54.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own receptivity to the word of God. Sometimes, we may be too familiar with Jesus' teachings to grasp their depth. Let us be attentive to the wisdom He offers us, even through means or people we consider ordinary, and open our hearts to his miracles in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'carpenter' and refers to a craftsman, often involved in construction. In the context of Jewish culture, a tektōn was not just a furniture maker but also a builder of houses, symbolizing manual labor and the dignity of work. Theologically, this underscores the humility of Jesus, who, although the Son of God, chose to live a life of labor and service.

This term means 'brother' and can also refer to a close relative or a member of the same community. In the context of this verse, it is used to refer to the brothers of Jesus, raising questions about the nature of his family. Spiritually, it can symbolize the community of believers, where Jesus is the firstborn among many brothers.

This word means 'mother' and evokes the fundamental role of motherhood in Jewish culture. Mary, as the mother of Jesus, is honored in Christian tradition, and her role underscores how God chose to intervene in human history. It also reminds us of the incarnation of Christ, who is fully God and fully man.

55.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in a context where Jesus was perceived by some as a mere man, the son of a carpenter, in a traditional Jewish society. Messianic expectations were high, and many sought a powerful king rather than a humble artisan.
55.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus teaches the crowds, but he faces the disbelief of those in Nazareth, his hometown. This verse highlights the difficulty people have in recognizing Jesus' divinity due to his origins and family background.
55.culture: In Jewish culture, lineage and family were of paramount importance. People were often judged by their origins, and the fact that Jesus was the son of a carpenter could make him less credible in the eyes of his contemporaries.
55.interpretation: This verse highlights the contrast between human perception and the divine reality of Jesus. While some see him as merely the son of a carpenter, he is in fact the Son of God, and this misunderstanding underscores the necessity of faith to recognize his true identity.
55.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Jesus, as the Son of God, chose to incarnate in humility and simplicity. It teaches us that God can act powerfully through what seems ordinary. As believers, we are called to recognize the divinity of Christ in our daily lives, even in the simplest moments.

mots.sens: This term means 'brother' and can also refer to a member of the same community or family. In the biblical context, it emphasizes the bonds of kinship and belonging. Spiritually, it evokes the idea of brotherhood among believers in Christ, reminding that all members of God's family are united by faith.

This word means 'with' and emphasizes proximity or association. In the context of this verse, it highlights the presence of Jesus' sisters in his company, suggesting a familiarity that can lead to mistrust or doubt. Theologically, it reminds us that even those who are close to us may struggle to recognize our divine calling.

This word means 'from where' and questions the origin or source of something. In this verse, it is used to question the provenance of Jesus' teachings and miracles. This raises reflections on the divine nature of Christ and how people can sometimes lack discernment in the face of God's work.

56.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during Jesus' earthly ministry, a time marked by messianic expectations and religious tensions in Israel.
56.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus teaches in parables and faces the disbelief of his fellow citizens in Nazareth. This verse illustrates the surprise and skepticism of the inhabitants regarding the miracles and wisdom of Jesus, whom they know as an ordinary man.
56.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued family ties and respect for traditions. People often had difficulty accepting that someone from their own background could be a prophet or the Messiah.
56.interpretation: This verse highlights the difficulty that those close to us have in recognizing God's work in the life of someone they know well. It sheds light on the human tendency to judge by appearances and to doubt divine authority when it manifests through familiar means.
56.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our faith can be tested by familiarity. It is essential to remain open to God's work, even when it comes from those we know. As believers, we must learn to discern God's voice beyond our prejudices and expectations, in order to recognize and accept his work in our lives and those of others.

mots.sens: This term refers to a 'prophet', a person chosen by God to convey His messages. The word has a root that evokes the idea of 'speaking for' or 'speaking beforehand', highlighting the individual's role as a divine spokesperson. In this verse, Jesus emphasizes that even prophets can be despised in their own environment, shedding light on the difficulty of accepting a familiar truth.

This word translates to 'stumbling block' or 'scandal'. It evokes something that causes offense or makes someone stumble in their faith. In the context of this verse, it underscores that the lack of faith among the inhabitants of Nazareth in the face of Jesus constitutes an obstacle to their reception of divine truth, illustrating how familiarity can breed contempt.

This term means 'homeland' or 'native country'. It refers to the idea of belonging and cultural identity. In the context of this verse, it highlights that contempt often comes from those who know a person best, illustrating the difficulty of accepting the spiritual authority of someone familiar.

57.epoque: In the time of Jesus, Jewish society was heavily marked by traditions and cultural expectations, where respect for teachers and prophets was essential, but often limited by familiarity and local prejudices.
57.passage: This verse is situated in a passage where Jesus returns to Nazareth, His hometown, after performing miracles and teaching with authority. Matthew chapter 13 presents various teachings and parables about the kingdom of heaven, and this verse highlights the resistance to faith that Jesus encounters from those who have known Him since childhood.
57.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, respect for authority figures, such as prophets, was important, but familiarity could breed contempt. This reveals a social dynamic where the acceptance of truth is often hindered by expectations and prejudices.
57.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God's truth can be rejected even by those closest to us. Jesus, as a prophet, exemplifies how prejudices can obscure the perception of divine truth, and it challenges us regarding our own receptivity to God's voice in our lives.
57.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of remaining open to truth, even when it comes from familiar sources. As believers, we must be careful not to let our familiarity with Jesus or His teachings lead us to despise or ignore them. It invites us to seek an authentic faith that can transcend our prejudices and expectations.

mots.sens: This term refers to unbelief or lack of faith. It comes from the root 'pisteuo', which means 'to have faith' or 'to believe'. In the context of this verse, the unbelief of the inhabitants of Nazareth prevented the manifestation of Jesus' miracles, thus emphasizing the importance of faith in receiving divine blessings. Spiritually, this reminds us that our heart's disposition can influence our experience of God's power.

This word means 'miracles' or 'wonders', and it is often associated with powerful acts of God that reveal His glory. In the New Testament, Jesus' miracles are signs of His divine authority and messianic mission. Their rarity in this passage underscores that God often acts in response to faith, and that unbelief can limit our experience of divine works.

The term 'topos' means 'place' or 'location'. In this verse, it refers to Nazareth, the hometown of Jesus. This choice of location is significant as it shows that even in a familiar place, faith can be absent, which can have consequences for God's work. It teaches us that our environment does not determine God's power, but our faith does.

58.epoque: This passage takes place in the 1st century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus in Palestine, a time marked by intense messianic expectation and religious tensions among different Jewish factions.
58.passage: In Matthew 13, Jesus teaches in parables and encounters varied reactions from the crowds. This verse highlights the resistance of His fellow townspeople in Nazareth to His message and miracles, illustrating the paradox of acceptance and rejection of divine truth.
58.culture: Nazareth was a small town where Jesus had grown up, and this proximity led to a lack of respect and recognition of His divine mission. This reflects a cultural mentality where familiarity can breed contempt, making it difficult to accept the novelty that Jesus brought.
58.interpretation: The unbelief of the inhabitants of Nazareth serves as a warning for us today. It reminds us that faith is essential to experience God's power in our lives. When we doubt or reject what God wants to do, we limit our own experience of His grace and miracles.
58.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of faith and open-mindedness in the face of God's work. Even in familiar places, where we might expect to see God act, our skepticism can hinder His power. Therefore, let us be vigilant in nurturing our faith and welcoming God's works in our lives, so as not to miss the miracles He desires to accomplish.
